## High-Performance Leadership and Management

### Research Journey and Findings

The authors' research journey included surveying technology professionals, publishing State of DevOps Reports with Puppet, researching technology transformations, and publishing results in peer review. A consistent finding across all research: since nearly every company relies on software, delivery performance is critical to any organization doing business today. Software delivery performance is affected by many factors including leadership, tools, automation, and a culture of continuous learning and improvement.

### Book Structure and Contributions

**Part I** presents research findings on why software delivery performance matters and how it drives organizational performance measures including profitability, productivity, market share, efficiency, effectiveness, customer satisfaction, and achieving mission goals. The ability to deliver quality software at high tempo with stability is described as a key value driver and differentiator for all organizations regardless of size or industry vertical.

**Part II** summarizes the science behind the research, including design decisions and analysis methods, providing the basis for the results discussed in the bulk of the text.

**Part III** discusses organizational change management. To present this material, the authors collaborated with colleagues Steve Bell and Karen Whitley Bell, whose contributed chapter presents one view of what following the capabilities and practices outlined in the book looks like and what it can provide for innovative organizations.

### Key Capabilities and Transformation

The authors identified key capabilities that contribute to software delivery performance in statistically significant and meaningful ways. Discussion of these practices with examples is intended to help readers improve their own performance.

### Path to High Performance

The authors emphasize that high performance cannot be bought or copied. Organizations must develop their own capabilities pursuing a path that fits their particular context and goals. This requires sustained effort, investment, focus, and time. The research is described as unequivocal: the results are worth it.

## The Imperative to Accelerate

Organizations across all industries—finance, retail, telecommunications, and government—are abandoning big projects with long lead times in favor of small teams working in short cycles with user feedback. These high performers focus relentlessly on delivering value, engaging the market to detect customer demand, anticipating compliance changes, and responding to risks like security threats or economic shifts.

## Software as Strategic Differentiator

Software is the central mechanism for delivering value in any industry. Banks no longer compete by holding gold in vaults but by trading faster and discovering new channels. Retailers win customers through superior selection, fast checkout, and seamless online/offline experiences—all enabled by technology. Research by Bessen (2017) confirms that strategic technology use explains revenue and productivity gains more than mergers, acquisitions, or entrepreneurship. McAfee and Brynjolfsson (2008) found a direct link between technology adoption and profitability.

## DevOps Transformation and Industry Gaps

DevOps practices are transforming organizations, though significant gaps remain. A Forrester report (Stroud et al. 2017) found 31% of organizations aren't using essential practices like continuous integration, continuous delivery, Lean methods, and collaborative culture. Meanwhile, 47% of CEOs face board pressure to digitally transform (Gartner, Panetta 2017). Organizations often overestimate their progress, with executives especially prone to this disconnect compared to practitioners closer to the work.

## Capabilities vs. Maturity Models

The key conceptual distinction is between maturity and capability models. Maturity models assume organizations "arrive" at a static endpoint and declare themselves done, whereas technology transformations require continuous improvement. Maturity models prescribe lock-step, linear formulas assuming all teams progress identically—but teams have their own context, systems, goals, and constraints. Capability models are multidimensional and dynamic, allowing customized approaches based on current context and short/long-term goals.

Capability models are outcome-based, tying improvements to business results rather than vanity metrics like technical proficiency or tooling install base. They also account for changing technology landscapes, allowing teams to focus on skills needed to remain competitive rather than targeting a fixed endpoint.

## Evidence-Based Capabilities

Our research identified 24 key capabilities that drive software delivery and organizational performance. Unlike factors like application age (mainframe vs. greenfield), whether operations or development performs deployments, or whether a change approval board exists, these capabilities predict success. They are easy to define, measure, and improve.

High performers demonstrate 46× more frequent deployments, 440× faster lead time from commit to deploy, 170× faster mean time to recover, and 5× lower change failure rates than low performers. The gap between high and low performers has widened over time, suggesting these capabilities create compounding competitive advantages. These 24 capabilities apply across all organization types and technology stacks worldwide.

## The Imperative to Accelerate

Organizations across all industries must shift from big projects with long lead times to small teams working in short cycles with user feedback. To remain competitive, organizations must accelerate delivery of goods and services, market engagement, anticipation of regulatory changes, and response to risks. Software is the key differentiator enabling this acceleration—banks compete through faster trading and new channels, retailers through superior selection and service enabled by technology.

## Focus on Capabilities, Not Maturity

The authors argue strongly against maturity models, identifying four key problems: (1) maturity models imply organizations "arrive" and stop improving, whereas technology transformations require continuous improvement; (2) maturity models prescribe lock-step, linear formulas assuming "Level 1" and "Level 2" look the same across all teams, but teams have unique contexts, systems, and constraints; (3) maturity models measure technical proficiency without tying it to outcomes, producing vanity metrics; (4) maturity models define static levels without accounting for the ever-changing technology landscape.

Capability models, by contrast, are multidimensional and dynamic, allowing customized improvement approaches focused on outcomes and key levers that drive improvement.

## Evidence-Based Transformations

A 2017 Forrester report found 31% of the industry is not using practices like continuous integration/delivery, Lean practices, and collaborative culture. A Gartner study found 47% of CEOs face board pressure to digitally transform. Research also shows executives overestimate their DevOps progress compared to practitioners.


The authors' research identified 24 key capabilities that drive software delivery and organizational performance. Notably, neither application age/technology (mainframe vs. greenfield), whether ops or dev performs deployments, nor whether a CAB is implemented predicted performance.


## High Performer Metrics (2017 vs. Low Performers)

High performers achieve: 46x more frequent deployments, 440x faster lead time from commit to deploy, 170x faster mean time to recover, and 5x lower change failure rate. The gap between high and low performers widened for stability metrics from 2016 to 2017, suggesting low performers increased tempo without building in quality. High performers understand they don't trade speed for stability—by building quality in, they get both.

Examples of successful transformations include Netflix, Amazon, Google, Facebook, Capital One, Target, and the US Federal Government's Technology Transformation Service and US Digital Service.
